prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its development into incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: B014 is the only ballot every member placed first, and that agreement rests on substance. It is a complete arc from gut-hormone physiology (proglucagon processing, the insulinotropic action of GLP-1) to long-acting agonists with demonstrated glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal benefit across large independent trials and years of real-world use. The discovery is physiological, the translation is documented, and the impact is already global, so I see no maturity concern. I keep Holst and Drucker as the scientific core and Knudsen as the person who made the biology into a usable drug.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is attribution. The credited list has four names and a prize holds three. Any trio omits a legitimate claimant, and the choice between Mojsov (identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1 peptide) and Knudsen (industrial development) is a real judgement about whether the prize rewards discovery or drug development. Habener-group contributions to proglucagon biology are not on the list at all. A prize that is seen as unfair on credit would damage an otherwise very strong case.

responses.point: Perlmann proposed Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, arguing that identifying and synthesising the active GLP-1 peptide is a discovery contribution that should be credited ahead of industrial development.
responses.response: I take this seriously and it is the main disagreement between my ballot and his. Mojsov's work on the active GLP-1(7-36) form is a discovery step, and I accept my trio leaves out a legitimate claimant. I still prefer Knudsen. The Nobel citation has to explain why GLP-1 is now a medicine, and without the long-acting analogues the physiology would not have reached patients. Holst and Drucker already carry the biological discovery, so the third place is better used for the translational step. I would change my view if the committee decides priority for the active peptide is clearly documented and the prize should stay with discovery. I cannot settle that from the supplied materials.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranked B039 second but narrowed it to June and Sadelain, noting that Rosenberg's adoptive transfer work is less central and that priority among early CAR concepts is unsettled.
responses.response: I agree that June and Sadelain are the strongest pair among those credited, and I would also drop Rosenberg from a CAR-T configuration. The attribution problem is wider than he notes. Eshhar's early chimeric receptor concept is not on the credited list, so a June and Sadelain prize would rest on names the ballot itself treats as incomplete. That is why I rank B039 as a very strong alternative and not as my first choice. Its attribution is less settled than B014's and the clinical benefit is concentrated in B-cell malignancies so far.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranked optogenetics (B036) second, with Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel, citing its causal, cell-type-specific control of neural activity across thousands of studies.
responses.response: Optogenetics matters a great deal to my own field, so I am wary of overweighting it and I scored it on the common criteria. As a tool it is transformative, but its disease-level medical impact is still limited to early vision restoration, which sits below B014 and B039 for a prize in Physiology or Medicine. Attribution is also harder: Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck are all strongly argued, and no three-person subset is defensible without excluding someone with a strong claim. I would not move it above B014, and I doubt it could be resolved for this year.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius also put Drucker, Holst and Mojsov on B014 and placed CAR-T and the unfolded protein response next, treating physiology, peptide identification and drug development as disputed shares.
responses.response: We agree on B014 and on Drucker and Holst. Her emphasis on the disputed division of credit is fair and I do not claim my three-person list is uncontested. Where I differ from her and Perlmann is in treating Mojsov as the better third name than Knudsen. I would want the committee to say explicitly whether the prize honours physiology plus therapy or physiology alone, because the answer settles the third name. I do not see a disagreement about the quality of the science.

uncertainties: Whether the third laureate should be Mojsov (peptide identification) or Knudsen (long-acting analogue development), which depends on how the committee weighs discovery against drug development. I have not checked the priority literature.
Contributions of Habener and colleagues to proglucagon biology are not credited on the ballot, and I cannot judge from the supplied materials whether they change the allocation.
Whether CAR-T (B039) could be framed with a clean three-person list given that Eshhar is not credited.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B014, B039 or B003. I have worked with Perlmann, as a 2009 co-author, and with Grillner and Ernfors, but none of them is a credited candidate on the shortlist. For B036 I use optogenetics as a methodological field, but I have no documented tie to any credited person.
